name: Aight
tagline: Native iOS and macOS control surface for self-hosted AI agents and coding CLIs

pricing.notes: Official pricing lists $4.99 monthly or $34.99 annually, with a free tier.

tiers.name: Free
tiers.limits: OpenClaw mode: 1 team, 8 agents and 2 group chats; Channels mode: 2 channels and 1 channel group; core chat.

tiers.name: Pro
tiers.limits: Unlimited teams, agents, group chats, channels and channel groups.
tiers.notes: $34.99/year; 3-day trial. Purchased through Apple's in-app purchase system.

pricing.freeTierCaps: 1 team, 8 agents, 2 group chats, 2 channels and 1 channel group
pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual through Apple in-app purchase; auto-renews unless cancelled at least 24 hours before renewal
pricing.hiddenCosts: Aight supplies only the client/control surface: it does not include AI models, agents or a backend, so model API charges and the self-hosted or cloud agent infrastructure are separate.

verdictSummary: A focused multi-backend iPhone prototype is a realistic multi-day build when a local companion normalizes each agent protocol, but hardening all four adapters plus Aight's hosted relay, voice, orchestration, sync, and App Store polish is multi-week product work.
coreLoopDIY: Build one SwiftUI client and a local adapter service that can start, resume, stream, interrupt, and approve work across Codex, Claude Code, OpenClaw, and Hermes.
requirements: at least one supported agent installed
whatYouLose: managed encrypted relay and push notifications
voice mode with local speech models
pre-built agent/team templates and community skill browsing
multi-device sync and App Store polish
whyPeopleStillPay: They pay for one polished client that safely reaches several agent backends from anywhere, keeps sessions in sync, and handles notifications, voice, and approvals without maintaining a custom mobile integration.

priorArt.name: Happy
priorArt.desc: Open-source mobile and web client for Codex and Claude Code with end-to-end encryption.

priorArt.name: CodexAppMobile
priorArt.desc: Open-source SwiftUI iOS client for a remote Codex app-server.

alternatives.name: Happy
alternatives.desc: A phone remote for Claude Code and Codex, with your computer still doing the work.

facts.install: Install the CLI with npm, launch an existing Claude Code or Codex session through Happy, then pair the mobile or web client
facts.engines: Claude Code and OpenAI Codex CLI; the underlying agent account and model access remain the user's
facts.dataFormat: Source code stays on the host computer; session messages and metadata are end-to-end encrypted through the Happy relay, with local CLI state under the user's home directory; the relay can be self-hosted
facts.gapVsPaid: Happy is a strong phone remote for Claude Code and Codex, but it lacks Aight’s OpenClaw and Hermes support, multi-agent group chats, voice modes, and built-in health and cost dashboards.
facts.setupBlocker: Requires Node.js, an already installed and authenticated Claude Code or Codex CLI, and a host computer that remains online

alternatives.name: Nimbalyst
alternatives.desc: A visual desk for several coding agents, without turning them into a node graph.

facts.install: Install the signed macOS DMG, Windows installer, or Linux AppImage and point it at already installed coding-agent CLIs
facts.engines: Codex and Claude Code, with OpenCode and GitHub Copilot support described as alpha
facts.dataFormat: Projects and planning artifacts are local-first and stored as ordinary files, including Markdown; optional sync and mobile access use Nimbalyst services
facts.gapVsPaid: Nimbalyst is a desktop agent workspace and does not provide Aight’s native iOS remote control, voice conversation, or multi-agent group-chat experience.
facts.setupBlocker: Requires at least one supported coding-agent CLI to be installed and authenticated separately

alternatives.name: Paseo
alternatives.desc: One control panel for five coding CLIs; the agents still need a host.

facts.install: Install the desktop app or CLI; its local daemon supervises installed agents, while optional remote clients pair to that host
facts.engines: Native support for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and Pi, plus a larger catalog including Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Amp, Aider, and custom ACP agents
facts.dataFormat: Repositories and agent processes remain on the host computer; clients communicate with a local daemon and, for remote access, an optional relay that can be self-hosted
facts.gapVsPaid: Paseo supports more terminal agents, but its daemon-and-client interface lacks Aight’s polished Apple-native voice, group-chat, gateway-health, and token-cost experience.
facts.setupBlocker: Requires supported agent CLIs to be installed and authenticated; remote control also requires pairing and an online host daemon

notes: The shared mobile control loop is buildable; maintaining four adapters and the polished remote experience is the hard part.
prompt:
Build me a local-first iPhone client for Codex, Claude Code, OpenClaw,
and Hermes. Requirements:

- Use Swift 6, SwiftUI, and iOS 18. Generate Xcode from a checked-in
  XcodeGen project.yml so `xcodegen && xcodebuild` works on a clean clone.
- Build the Node.js 22 TypeScript companion with Fastify and WebSockets. Expose
  start, resume, prompt, event, approval, interrupt, and capability operations;
  session listing is optional and capability-gated.
- Ship real adapters for all four. Disable unavailable agents at runtime; all
  adapters must compile and pass fixture tests without every agent installed.
- Codex: pin the CLI version, run `codex app-server generate-ts`, and supervise
  app-server over stdio using the generated v2 types.
- Claude Code: use `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk`, its session APIs,
  async-iterable input for interrupt(), and canUseTool for permissions.
- OpenClaw: use the official Gateway WebSocket client, pair once, request only
  read/write/approvals/questions scopes, and store its device token securely.
- Hermes: use /v1/runs and its event, approval, and stop endpoints; use
  session headers for continuity and discover features from /v1/capabilities.
- Keep backend models in the companion and expose one versioned protocol. The
  iOS app stores its wss:// endpoint and bridge bearer token in Keychain.
- Provide backend/session pickers, streamed Markdown and tool events, approval
  cards, Stop, capability-aware controls, and deny approvals on disconnect.
- Bind to 127.0.0.1 and compare the random `.env` token in constant time;
  expose it only through private Tailscale Serve HTTPS, and never enable Funnel.
- Add bounded reconnects and local completion notifications. No app accounts,
  cloud database, analytics, or telemetry; agent model-provider calls remain.
- Out of scope: hosted relay, voice, cross-backend groups, templates, community
  skills, themes, multi-device sync, and a macOS client.
- Test adapter fixtures plus denial, interruption, and reconnection. README:
  setup for all four, `.env.example`, Tailscale, signing, permissions, limits.
